Maybe make it a little less daunting. “Come on!” Leon went first. He lowered himself in without ceremony, one hand on the wall, keeping his eyes forward and slightly up the way he'd been doing since the hallway. Not looking at the water. Definitely not thinking about the particular quality of dark water, the way it closed over your shoulders like something deciding, the specific cold of a lake in summer that shouldn't have been cold but was— He moved through it efficiently. Hand on the wall, feet finding the floor on the other side, up and out. Simple. Done. David followed slower, sliding into the hole with a soft curse and kicking across it with mechanical rhythm. His limbs felt heavier in the water than they should. He didn’t like it. Didn’t like the silence, or the drag, or the way the space bent around them. But he made it. Dwight whined once, a low pained sound in the depths of his chest, before following David. The water lapped gently at his legs as the others waited on the far side. His hands trembled at his sides, stomach clenching uncomfortably, then settled into a low grumble. The last time he was in there had been absolute hell. Last time the dark had been complete and the water had been warm and patient and something had kept bumping his legs in the— He got in. This time, at least... there were eyes on him. David's hand found his arm on the other side before he'd even asked for it, hauling him up onto solid tile. His whole frame shook as he pulled free from the water. Jake watched the others come up on the far side, dripping and breathing hard, and mentally measured the gap. The pressure in the wall shifted slightly and he side-eyed it for a moment, before tucking the crowbar into his belt and stepping forward. The edge of the tile shifted under his foot. Not dramatically — just a subtle wrongness under his leading foot, the tile angling wrong in a way that registered a half-second too late, then there was no floor. He didn’t even get out a full warning. Just a single, startled “Shit—!” as the water closed over his head and the hole took him. “Jake?!” Orela’s light jerked toward the surface, but it only caught ripples. “Jake!” Dwight moved on pure reflex, already leaning toward the gap before his brain had caught up with what was happening, and Orela's hand caught his arm and yanked him back hard enough to stagger him. "Don't—" He froze. Teetered. The edge was gone again. “He’s not... he was right there!” David was already stepping forward. "I'll get him—" "No—!" The word came out of Dwight sharper than he'd intended, sharp enough to stop David mid-step. He didn't know where it came from. He just knew, with a certainty that sat in his chest like something physical, that David going back into that water was not something he could let happen. Orela’s jaw clenched. She shoved her flashlight into Leon’s hands, voice low and steady even as her knuckles shook. "David’s injured. You’re the faster swimmer out of us. You’ve got the best chance. Find him." Leon stared at the light for half a second too long, then down at the black water yawning in front of him. His jaw tightened. The universe, he thought, had a very specific and deeply personal sense of humor. Of course it would be him. It was just his luck. He'd prevented the end of the world more times than he could count on one hand and apparently the lesson the cosmos had taken from that was this guy can handle anything, let's keep testing it. The lake water surfaced briefly in the back of his mind and he put it down. He obviously wasn’t going to leave Jake behind. He handed Orela his vest, checked his grip on the flashlight, took a few steadying breaths, dove clean, and vanished beneath the surface. The darkness swallowed the beam almost immediately. The others watched the light sink below the surface and disappear, and then there was nothing. Just the water lapping softly at the edge of the hole and five people minus one standing very still in the dark. Nobody moved. The floor had already demonstrated what it thought about people who moved. Dwight counted his own heartbeats and tried not to think about the last time he'd been waiting for someone to come back up through a hole in the floor. That time everything had happened fast, the water rising, the clock obvious and urgent. This was slower. The waiting stretched and the dark pressed in and slow, it turned out, was its own particular kind of terrible. David cursed gently to himself, trying to calm the reflexive itch in his lungs. Dwight's outcry rang sharp in his mind, and for a moment he was back in the basement; lost, panicked, flailing at everything rhythm touched him. Dwight had nearly lost him down there, and he just tried to go right back in without even thinking. His own bull-headed reflexes were causing pain on others. They were already scared enough. He needed to get them out before it got worse. Orela stared at the spot where she had last seen the light and tried not to second guess herself. Leon had gone in reluctantly — she'd seen it, the particular quality of his hesitation, something underneath the pragmatism that he wasn't going to name and she wasn't going to ask about. He seemed to be struggling with something beyond just the darkness and the rising threat. The man clearly had baggage; Orela had seen that look before.
